title: Food Chains and Food Webs
seo_title: Year 4 Science: Food Chains and Food Webs Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Explain the roles and interactions of consumers, producers and decomposers within a habitat and how food chains represent feeding relationships (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 4 science worksheets on food chains and food webs in Australian habitats: the bush, a billabong, the Great Barrier Reef and the outback. Producers, predators and prey. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Arrows go from the food to the eater.
key_sub: A food chain starts with a producer; a food web joins many chains.
body_html:
How to think about it

A food chain shows what eats what. The arrow points from the food to the animal that eats it.

  • Every chain starts with a producer (a plant or algae) that uses sunlight to make food.
  • Consumers eat other living things: herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat animals, omnivores eat both.
  • A food web joins many chains. If one population changes, others change too.
Example

Grass → kangaroo → dingo. Which is the producer?

the chain starts with the plant

Answer: grass

Example

Dingoes are removed. Kangaroos?

fewer predators eat them

Answer: more kangaroos at first

Common mistakes

  • Drawing arrows from the eater to the food.
  • Putting the producer at the end of the chain.
  • Thinking that removing a predator makes every population fall.

faq.q: Which way do arrows go in a food chain?
faq.a: From the food to the eater. The arrow shows the direction the energy moves: grass → kangaroo means the kangaroo eats the grass.

faq.q: What is the difference between a food chain and a food web?
faq.a: A food chain is one path of feeding. A food web joins many food chains because most animals eat more than one kind of food.

faq.q: What happens if one animal disappears from a food web?
faq.a: Its prey may increase and its predators may decrease or switch to other food. One change can affect many living things.

items.q: Which living thing is always at the start of a food chain?
c: a producer, such as a plant
items.e: Producers make their own food.

items.q: In the food chain native grass → grasshopper → bearded dragon → goanna, which animal is the top predator?
items.e: The top predator is at the end of the chain; nothing in the chain eats it.

an animal at the end of a food chain that nothing in the chain eats

items.q: Can an animal be both predator and prey?
c: Yes, for example a blue tit eats caterpillars but is eaten by sparrowhawks.

items.q: Why are decomposers important in a food web?
c: They break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil for plants.
items.e: Nutrients are recycled.

items.q: An animal eats both plants and animals. What is it called?
items.e: Omni- means all.

items.q: Look at the food web of a billabong. A disease kills most of the waterweed. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The yabby eats only waterweed in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: What does a food chain show?
c: which living thing is eaten by which, and how energy passes along
items.e: Energy passes from the food to the eater.

items.q: What is a producer?
c: a fungus that breaks down dead things
a plant that makes its own food using light
items.e: Every food chain starts with a producer.

items.q: What does a food chain show?
c: what eats what, and how energy passes from one living thing to another
items.e: Energy passes along the chain.

items.q: Look at the food web of a bushland habitat. A disease kills most of the mice. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The brown snake eats only a mouse in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: In the chain grass → kangaroo → dingo, which is the prey of the dingo?
items.e: Prey is the animal eaten.

items.q: Which statement about energy in a food chain is correct?
c: Energy passes from the producer to the consumers.
Energy passes from the top predator to the plant.
Energy is created by each animal.
items.e: It flows in the direction of the arrows.

items.q: Look at the food web of an outback desert. Most of the dingoes are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the dingo eats red kangaroos in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: Why are there usually more producers than top consumers?
c: Top consumers make their own food.
Energy is lost at each step, so less energy reaches the top.
items.e: Only part of the energy is passed on.

items.q: Look at the food web of a billabong. Most of the dragonfly nymphs are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the dragonfly nymph eats mosquito larvae in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: Look at the food web of an outback desert. Most of the red kangaroos are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the red kangaroo eats saltbush in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: Look at the food web of an outback desert. A disease kills most of the native grass. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The ant eats only native grass in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: Can an animal be both a predator and prey?
c: Yes. A mudskipper eats snails but is eaten by kingfishers.
items.e: Many animals are both.

items.q: Look at the food web of an outback desert. A disease kills most of the ants. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
items.e: The thorny devil eats only an ant in this web, so it loses its food.

items.q: What is a consumer?
c: an animal that gets energy by eating other living things
items.e: Consumers cannot make their own food.

items.q: What would happen to a food web if all the producers died?
c: All the consumers would eventually die from lack of food.
items.e: Every chain starts with a producer.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Most of the coral trout are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the coral trout eats small fish in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: Which organisms break down dead plants and animals?
c: decomposers such as bacteria and fungi
items.e: They return nutrients to the soil.

items.q: Look at the food web of a bushland habitat. Which of these does the grasshopper eat?
items.e: The arrow points from the food to the grasshopper.

items.q: Look at the food web of an outback desert. Which of these does the thorny devil eat?
items.e: The arrow points from the food to the thorny devil.

items.q: A drought kills much of the grass in the outback. Which animals are affected first?
c: herbivores such as kangaroos and grasshoppers
items.e: Herbivores depend directly on plants.

items.q: In the food chain leaves → caterpillar → magpie, which animal is the top predator?
items.e: The top predator is at the end of the chain; nothing in the chain eats it.

items.q: Why are food chains in real habitats joined into food webs?
c: Most animals eat more than one kind of food.
items.e: Many links.

items.q: In a food chain, what is a predator?
c: a living thing that hunts and eats other animals
a living thing that eats only plants
a living thing that makes its own food using energy from sunlight
a living thing that gets its energy by eating other living things
items.e: Learn the food chain words.

items.q: Owls cough up pellets of bones and fur. What can scientists learn from them?
c: what the owl has been eating
items.e: Evidence of diet.

items.q: Dingoes are removed from an area. Which change is most likely at first?
items.e: With fewer predators, prey numbers rise.

items.q: Why can a fall in the number of bees affect many animals?
c: Bees pollinate plants that many animals depend on for food.
items.e: Living things depend on each other.

items.q: Jack writes: koala → gum tree. What is wrong?
c: Koalas do not eat gum leaves.
The arrow points the wrong way; it should be gum tree → koala.
items.e: Arrows go from food to eater.

items.q: Why do scientists study food webs before letting a new animal into an area?
c: A new animal can change the numbers of many other living things.
To find the best colour of animals.
items.e: Cane toads are an example of a harmful introduction.

items.q: The number of mosquitoes in a pond fell after guppies were added. Why?
c: Guppies eat adult mosquitoes in the air.
items.e: Guppies are used to control mosquito breeding.

items.q: In the food chain banksia flowers → honey possum, which living thing is the producer?
items.e: The producer makes its own food from sunlight and comes first.

items.q: In a food chain, what is a producer?
c: a living thing that hunts and eats other animals
a living thing that is hunted and eaten by other animals
a living thing that makes its own food using energy from sunlight

items.e: Learn the food chain words.

items.q: In the food chain phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → coral trout → reef shark, which living thing is the producer?
items.e: The producer makes its own food from sunlight and comes first.

items.q: Look at the food web of an outback desert. Which of these does the bearded dragon eat?
items.e: The arrow points from the food to the bearded dragon.

items.q: Mei counted the animals in a school garden: 120 aphids, 15 ladybirds. Why are there more aphids than ladybirds?
c: Each ladybird eats many aphids, and less energy reaches the ladybirds.
items.e: Prey usually outnumber predators.

items.q: Farmers released ladybirds into a vegetable farm with many aphids. What is the most likely result?
items.e: Ladybirds are predators of aphids.

items.q: In a food chain, what is a carnivore?
c: a living thing that is hunted and eaten by other animals
a living thing that makes its own food using energy from sunlight
a living thing that eats only animals
a living thing that eats only plants
items.e: Learn the food chain words.

items.q: Mia counts animals at a billabong: 200 tadpoles, 30 dragonfly nymphs, 2 platypuses. What pattern does she see?
c: All levels have the same number.
There are fewer animals higher up the food chain.
There are more animals at the top.
items.e: Energy is lost at each step, so fewer animals can be supported.
